content:
Every AI model you use has a hard expiration date, and this Stanford professor just showed the class exactly why feeding it more text doesn't fix it

GPT-5's knowledge simply stops on September 30, 2024. Ask it anything after that, and it either goes silent or makes something up

His wildest reveal: even with a massive 400,000-token context window, just dumping everything into the prompt actively makes the model dumber. 

Researchers ran a "needle in a haystack" test and found models routinely lose facts buried in the first half of a long prompt, even when nothing is technically missing

His blunt explanation for why nobody just retrains the model instead: "it's very tricky to change the knowledge of an LLM without causing regression on other things." Companies avoid it entirely

The fix behind every modern AI product you use, RAG, boils down to three brutally simple steps: retrieve the right chunk of information, stuff it into the prompt, then generate the answer. That's the entire trick behind making an AI "know" things it was never trained on

Agents don't have bank accounts.

But they can have access to one.

@base MCP is making that idea feel surprisingly simple: connect a Base Account to an AI interface like Claude or ChatGPT, then let the agent handle onchain actions through chat.

It can check balances, track your portfolio, send funds, swap tokens and interact with apps like Uniswap, Morpho, Aerodrome and Moonwell.

The important part? The agent never gets your private keys.

Whenever an action needs to happen, it sends the transaction to your Base Account. You review what will change, then approve or reject it yourself.

That creates a pretty interesting shift for the Base ecosystem.

Instead of opening ten different apps to do something onchain, the agent can become the interface between users and the entire ecosystem.

And this is probably just the beginning.

If agents are going to become a real part of how people use crypto, giving them a safe way to interact with onchain apps feels like one of the pieces that had to exist.

Base MCP is starting to put that piece in place.

content:
alright - Grok Bot

i just spent quite some time with it since its introduction yesterday, did a bunch of work, and here's my real experience and initial thoughts

1. it's a very capable product packaged behind an extremely simple user interface

remember Buzz? that app gave me the opposite impression, which was a few simple pieces of technology put together into a complex and somewhat disorienting experience

if I am to reverse-PM Grok Bot, i would say it's targeting an average knowledge worker who doesn't have technical background and couldn't care less about clis, skills, context window, tokens, mcp, memory, cloud sandboxes, secrets, cron jobs etc etc, and just want a powerful agent that can actually get some work done

and i'd say it's done a fantastic job at designing for that audience. all the complexity is well hidden - the user only sees the bots, and get most things done by talking to them

as i revealed in my previous tweet, grok bot was clearly built by cursor and rebranded to grok - it speaks to the strength of cursor's product team there

2. next i'll reverse-engineer it a bit as well

Grok Bot gives every user one virtual machine in the cloud. both the mac app and the ios app are just a thin client that communicate with bots in the cloud VM

all the same users' bots share this same VM resource, but each bot has its own virtual desktop so they won't compete on the GUI interactions

the VM has 8 vCPU cores, 16GB of RAM and 128 GB of disk running a debian system, which is plenty for knowledge work. if you rent an equivalent of this machine from most cloud providers it can cost ~$200/month give or take for each full month, which is too high of an operational cost, so there must have be some optimizations done to hibernate/resume the VM automatically. this probably has some abuse vectors - some people will absolutely run the machine as a free VPS to do other things

even then, this machine is not sufficient if you want to do a lot of coding work which needs to run resource intensive tasks like build, test etc. but.. it seems they have already thought of that - coding work can be delegated to cursor cloud agents, not in the Grok Bot VM itself

each bot is an instance of an agent harness running in the VM. this harness doesn't look like the same as Cursor. it's something called "Sand". if you ask it, it'll tell you and even show you its current JS code

because the harness runs in a real VM environment, it's able to work with anything - CLIs, MCP, code execution, skills etc - which provides the foundation for an agent that's pretty much as powerful as the ones we run locally

3. many people are complaining about the pricing

don't worry about that - and i'll tell you why by reverse-GTM this as well

it's clear that the product is designed for all the average knowledge workers whose usage wouldn't be as heavy as developers who run many agent loops all day. people who just need to summarize some emails once in a while will never pay for $200+ a month, and there's no way the team doesn't already know this

the reason they are only providing access to ultra and supergrok heavy subscribers is that they want the first wave of adopters to be the power users and tinkerers (like me) who will play with the product meaningfully, can give them feedback, and will not churn even if the product has rough edges. through this phase they can also test the reliability, scalability and cost efficiency of their system, to develop more confidence in a broader rollout

i'm pretty sure in a few weeks they will relax the gating and give access to subscribers at lower pricing points, and open up to teams and enterprises as well

4. where it can improve

to be honest - i'm an engineer, so i'm not exactly representative of the target audience, but i'm going to share my reactions anyway:

- i wish i can see what model is being used. i don't want to have a bot touch a critical task unless i know it's using a big model :)

given how fast the agent responds (which is a good thing), i often have the worry it's running a cheap open source model for efficiency purpose that might screw things up

if the goal is to hide complexity, consider having an intelligence slider or something for power users to have some visibility and agency would go a long way

- the bots currently are designed to be "persistent". for example, it looks like a bot can create other bots, but can't delete them

this limitation made it hard for me to replicate @myfirstmate experience in there

i think it would be better to think of bots as a primitive in the system and allow full agentic control over them. at the very least, if bot A created bot B, then give A permission to delete B. this can open up a whole new door for power users to create any freeform multi-agent system without constraints

- i started moving a bunch of my regular tasks into Grok Bot, but one thing did give me a pause - it's vendor lock-in

unlike hermes and openclaw where i own all my stuff, once i moved my workloads into Grok Bot, i'm tied to their subscription and if one day i want to use another LLM subscription instead, it would be harder to make the switch

to ease this concern, an "export" flow would be helpful. it would be slightly against their business to do so, but it's a tradeoff between retaining users who actually want to leave vs allowing users who want to join to have one less thing to worry about before they do - the choice is actually clear

alright - that's most of my thoughts for now! overall, i'm really impressed. this is a well-executed agent product that has a lot of depth deliberately and carefully curated behind a simple interface. i look forward to what's coming next!

title: I gave Codex access to a clean @DigitalMeld Microsoft 365 and Azure dev tenant and asked it to build BusinessMeld, our internal decision-and-follow-through application - that we can access from from B
content:
I gave Codex access to a clean @DigitalMeld Microsoft 365 and Azure dev tenant and asked it to build BusinessMeld, our internal decision-and-follow-through application - that we can access from from Buzz or Microsoft Teams.

The application is a responsive Power Apps Code App backed by Dataverse. Dataverse owns BusinessMeld’s Decision Items, evidence snapshots, Accountable Owners, Priority Bands, proposals, dispositions, execution receipts, audit events, research, financial projections, integration state, and configuration.

Codex did all of the heavy lifting, including:
• Dataverse tables, relationships, alternate keys, choices, auditing, and security roles
• Server-side plug-ins enforcing immutability, idempotency, source freshness, retention, consent, and authorization
• Custom APIs exposing tightly governed operations to internal agents
• Power Automate flows for DealMeld (our custom CRM, contract, and project tool) synchronization, QuickBooks reconciliation, Teams delivery, retention, and integration recovery
• Environment variables and connection references so configuration is not embedded in the application
• A complete Power Platform solution containing the app, schema, flows, connectors, roles, and configuration

Microsoft Entra ID handles authentication and workload identity. A dedicated Buzz application identity can submit bounded research and proposals, but it can't impersonate a Team Member, contact anyone, publish anything, modify QuickBooks, or make decisions.

Microsoft Graph and Azure CLI were used to configure and verify those identities, inspect application credentials, and remove temporary credentials after testing. Azure is primarily the identity and governance plane here; the BusinessMeld runtime itself lives in Power Platform rather than Azure Functions, App Service, or a VM.

DealMeld remains the authoritative relationship system. BusinessMeld reads bounded, versioned relationship context and can create only controlled, non-sending handoffs we approve. Every handoff requires expected-version protection, an idempotency key, and a receipt.

QuickBooks remains the accounting authority, as the custom connector exposes only GET operations. A solution-owned synchronization process handles OAuth, rotating refresh tokens, pagination, reconciliation, and current A/R, A/P, and cash projections. The latest full run read thousands of records, retained hundreds of projections, deleted nothing, and completed reconciliation without introducing an accounting write path.

Microsoft Teams is delivery pane of glass, BusinessMeld sends private daily digests and only specifically approved urgent notifications. Deliveries are deduplicated and recorded with immutable receipts and deep links back to the app.

Power Platform DLP restricts custom connectors to the exact approved DealMeld and QuickBooks URL patterns and blocks everything else. The environment also has least-privilege roles, separate connections, audited configuration, a recoverable backup, and retention rules that remove replicated descriptive content while preserving minimum non-content tombstones.

The current release has passed hundreds of controlled scenarios covering the complete decision loop, all operating lanes, source failures, conflicts, replay, redaction, accessibility, and responsive layouts. Live checks have also passed for Dataverse, DealMeld, QuickBooks, Teams, the governed Buzz boundary, recovery, DLP, and Brad’s authenticated Power Apps session... whew.

All of this was done with Codex and GPT 5.6 Sol on High, nearly fully hands off, using my recently released AI-Native Operating framework, and the grill-with-docs to create a PRD and a MVP issue backlog. 

Long story short, Codex can do far more than throw together an app. With a clear product model, source-of-truth documentation, explicit authority boundaries, reviewable issues, and live verification, it can perform a surprising amount of real Microsoft cloud engineering.

That includes: identity, permissions, OAuth, DLP, retries, receipts, auditing, retention, deployment, cleanup, and proving that the system behaves correctly after it reaches the tenant.

Our AI-Native Operating Framework was the foundation this was built on - https://t.co/Wi83itzZVP

And now we begin the operational pilot, and user feedback loop.

content:
Mark Zuckerberg just gave away the highest performing model of its size in the world. It runs on your laptop.

Zuckerberg: “I think the key to building a positive future for everyone is to make sure that everyone has access to personal super intelligence.”

Access is the entire claim. Everything else in the announcement serves it.

Zuckerberg: “I am proud to share that we are open sourcing a new class of on-device models that we are calling Muse Glimmer. It’s a thirty billion parameter dense model that runs on your laptop, and it’s the highest performing model of its size.”

A model on your own machine answers to you.

It works with the wifi off, leaves no record anywhere else, and costs nothing per question.

Zuckerberg: “In the coming weeks, we are also going to open the weights for Muse Spark 1.2, our latest foundation model and one of the leading models in the world.”

That one matters more. A small model going out is a product decision. The frontier model following it is a commitment.

Zuckerberg: “Another part of building a positive future for everyone is making sure that everywhere we build infrastructure, local communities benefit.”

The compute behind all of this sits somewhere specific. Land, power, water, and a county that has to agree to host it.

Mill towns and refinery towns carried that weight for a century while the output shipped somewhere wealthier. The arrangement is old enough to be the default.

Zuckerberg: “We’ve already seen this with the teachers in Richland Parish who got fifty thousand dollar bonuses because of the extra tax revenue from our investments, and we’ve launched America’s Workforce Academy to provide free training and guaranteed jobs at our infrastructure sites.”

Fifty thousand dollars changes a teacher’s life in rural Louisiana. It arrived because the machine was built down the road.

Zuckerberg: “We’re starting a new Future is for Everyone fund to invest in the community’s teachers, first responders, energy and water infrastructure, and more ways to support those communities directly.”

Teachers, first responders, energy and water. Those are the things a town needs whether or not a datacenter ever gets built there.

Zuckerberg: “We’re also working to make sure that everyone has a personal super intelligence agent that works 24/7 on your behalf to improve your health, your relationships, your career, your finances, and more.”

Both ends of that have to hold at once. Somebody hosts the plant, and everybody else gets what it makes.

The hardware has an address. What comes out of it has none.

content:
The Future Is for Everyone: My Take On  Mark Zuckerberg’s Vision of Personal Superintelligence.

I am neutral to negative about Mark Zuckerberg the person. I have no particular affinity for Meta as a company or its history. What I respond to is the vision itself.

On August 10, 2026, Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word manifesto titled *The Future is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future*. You can read it here: [https://t.co/ElTNJs8pN0].

The core claim is straightforward and powerful: superintelligence should not be concentrated in the hands of a few labs, governments, or institutions. It should be delivered as personal superintelligence to billions of people so that each individual can direct it toward their own goals, values, and aspirations. The philosophy rests on three pillars: individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, invention as the primary purpose of superintelligence, and balance of power as the foundation of safety.

This is the vision I support.

Here are the top ten points that stand out, presented as clearly as I can extract and affirm them.

1. Personal agents that actually know you
Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands their goals, context, relationships, health, career, finances, and hobbies. The agent works 24/7 on the individual’s behalf. Zuckerberg’s own examples are telling: it monitors sleep and training, flags useful information, prototypes ideas, and even plans weekend baking with his daughter, ordering ingredients and offering suggestions in real time. This is not a chatbot. It is a continuous, context-aware partner.

2. Individual empowerment over institutional control 
“Putting power in people’s hands to pursue their own aspirations is how humanity has made the most progress.” Novel ideas rarely originate solely from established institutions. When every person has powerful tools, each becomes more capable of shaping the future rather than less.

3. Invention, not mere automation, as the primary purpose
The greatest contribution of superintelligence will not be replacing human labor but generating an unlimited number of valuable new things people can invent to achieve their goals. Abundance of intelligence should expand the frontier of what is possible, not simply optimize the existing map.

4. Balance of power through broad distribution
There is no singular benevolent superintelligence that can serve every competing set of human values. If the technology is held by a small number of individuals, businesses, governments, or the AI itself, outcomes will favor those holders. The safer and more prosperous path is many different superintelligent agents aligned to different people, competing and checking one another the way free people and free institutions do.

5. Open models as a force for empowerment and security
Meta intends to resume releasing open-weight models. Open systems allow more people to inspect, harden, improve, and build upon them. Concentration behind closed walls is not inherently safer; history suggests the opposite once the technology is sufficiently capable.

6. Free or affordable access at massive scale
The goal is to deliver personal superintelligence to billions of people and small businesses, offering free or low-cost versions and using dynamic auction mechanisms for additional compute so that price stays as low as possible. The benefits must be distributed widely if the vision is to hold.

7. Real privacy architecture
Agents will support a fully private mode in which even the service provider (Meta included) cannot see or grant access to the user’s information—modeled on the encryption approach used in WhatsApp. Without this, trust collapses and the personal nature of the system becomes a liability rather than an asset.

8. More entrepreneurship and more employment over time, not less
The prediction is not a world of fewer jobs overall but a world with a larger number of smaller companies and one-person product studios. Personal tutors and coaches with PhD-level knowledge in every subject, combined with powerful creation tools, will help people adapt, invent, and start new things. Historical technological leaps have expanded total prosperity and work even as specific roles disappeared.

9. Infrastructure that actually benefits the communities that host it
Data centers and power build-outs must deliver high-paying local jobs, training (including a proposed America’s Workforce Academy), tax revenue that supports teachers and public services, energy price stability, and environmental commitments such as water positivity. A “Future Is For Everyone Fund” is proposed to make this concrete.

10. Collaboration with government on genuine risks without defaulting to centralization
Frontier labs should share intermediate training checkpoints with government for review on critical areas such as cybersecurity of infrastructure. The aim is proactive partnership rather than rigid, late-stage gatekeeping that slows public access or concentrates power further. American leadership in open capabilities is framed as strategically important for democratic values.

The manifesto is explicit that Meta’s focus is personal superintelligence for individuals and small businesses, while many competitors are optimizing primarily for institutions and enterprises. That difference in primary customer is not trivial; it shapes the entire trajectory of the technology.

I have been saying versions of this for two decades.

Long before the current wave of large language models, I argued that the real leverage of AI would come when capable systems lived close to the individual knowing their history, goals, and context and could act as continuous partners rather than remote oracles controlled by a handful of organizations. 

I have written about personal knowledge systems that compound over decades, about distributed rather than centralized intelligence, about agents that serve the person first, and about the danger of concentrating powerful tools in too few hands. 

The garage-lab ethic, the insistence on local and personal control where possible, the framing of technology as a bicycle for the mind rather than a replacement for human agency these have been consistent themes.

Zuckerberg’s manifesto does not invent this direction. It finally states it at industrial scale from a company with the resources and distribution reach to attempt it. 

Whether Meta will actually deliver on the privacy guarantees, the open releases, the community benefits, and the genuine distribution of power remains to be proven in execution. Visions are cheap; follow-through is expensive.

But the vision itself is correct in its fundamental direction. Superintelligence that remains the exclusive tool of a few institutions will amplify existing power imbalances. 

Superintelligence that reaches billions of individuals as personal agents aligned to their own goals has a chance to expand human agency on a scale we have not seen before.

That is the future worth building toward. I am skeptical about the delivery. But the ideal to democratize AI should be applauded because it is not at all what we get from Anthropic or OpenAI.

NVIDIA LAUNCHES ITS MOST EFFICIENT OPEN AI MODEL

Nvidia has joined the open AI support club, launching Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, its own model. 

It contains knowledge from Nvidia’s powerful models packaged smaller in size. This makes it cheaper for routine tasks but also more efficient.

They also launched Switchyard, a router that automatically sends simple tasks to smaller models and complex work to powerful ones.

It was originally built to control its own token costs and protect its IP, but is now available to other companies.

Their internal testing showed Switchyard had similar accuracy just at one-third the cost of the Opus 4.8 model.

While an external test by LangChain showed costs reduced by 74%, but accuracy fell 6%.

Companies can customize and self-train the open model. This helps them control token costs while keeping sensitive data and intellectual property within their own systems.

The launch comes a day after Meta released its own open model, Muse Glimmer.

As Chinese open models compete to become the global foundation for AI, open models are becoming critical to America’s AI race.

Marginal delay (spent well) reduces risk but delays benefits. So when is risk red
content:
How long should we delay ASI to cut the chance of misaligned AI takeover? (Given a stable US-China deal like Plan A.)

Marginal delay (spent well) reduces risk but delays benefits. So when is risk reduction outweighed by delayed benefit?

Perhaps ~0.25% reduction / year of delay. More precisely, my guess is that a reasonable aggregate of human preferences would be roughly indifferent between a 0.25% absolute takeover risk reduction and delaying the benefits of wildly superhuman AIs by a year. Personally, my own preferences would put the number somewhat lower, since I'm pretty longtermist (caring a lot about the lives of people in the far future).

How'd I get this estimate? Well, around 0.75% of people die each year. So this would get you 0.75% reduction / year of delay if you just care about saving the lives of currently alive people (in a rolling way) and assume misaligned AI takeover kills everyone.

However, people also care about the lives of their children, the future, and generally put more emphasis on everyone getting to live a decently long life than on radical life extension. But, misaligned AI takeover maybe only kills half of people in expectation, though with some chance of an outcome for people that they'd consider much worse than death.

So totaling up these considerations, maybe a better estimate is 0.25%. I'd be sympathetic to numbers more like 0.75% or 1% and to numbers more like 0.01%, but numbers like 5% seem wild under most plausible ethical/moral perspectives.

I'm imagining that we "spend" delay on things like: putting more effort into safety/alignment relative to capabilities, making sure we have adequate control measures and society level defenses, and just making sure humans have time to understand what is going on. In practice, any delays will probably be highly suboptimal, potentially even counterproductive.

Also, I think we won't be able to hit the right tradeoff even given good decision making, as the risk that the governance regime collapses (and ASI is built in a worse situation) will probably outweigh the (high) risks of proceeding. (See discussion in "AI 2040: Plan A".) And in practice, I don't expect us to successfully get a decent governance regime at all...

So when thinking about highly ambitious but still at all potentially practical governance regimes, I'm guessing you're probably going to end up with an effective threshold more like 1-3% risk reduction per year of delay in practice (keep in mind this is the optimistic case!). (Though people might be very confused about the actual tradeoffs.) And I think in the median world a well-spent year of delay might cut risk by around 15%. Obviously, this depends a lot on my view that misaligned AI takeover risk is pretty high by default!

So, I expect that we'll fail to delay the right amount, but we could actually do a decent job carefully considering this question and making good tradeoffs. (Though this might require that people roughly agree on risk estimates.)

content:
Had @RyanGreenblatt on to discuss/debate recursive self-improvement.

This might be the most important question in the world right now - whether within a year or so of achieving human level intelligence, you slingshot towards having 10s of billions of superintelligences, each of which is dramatically more competent than human experts across all fields.

I’ve historically been skeptical of this possibility. My intuition has been that we will end up significantly bottlenecked by not only compute scaling but human expert data, which I think underlies most of the AI progress today.

If, because of RSI, we got a jump as big as GPT-3 to a Mythos (i.e. 6 years of AI progress) within a single year of achieving AGI, then the thing we get there at the end of that year is definitively and wildly superhuman.

We hashed it out, and I think Ryan made a pretty good case that this kind of speedup is plausible. FWIW, Ryan’s median for when we automate AI R&D is 2031.

We then discussed the alignment implications of this scenario. Who should these superintelligences be aligned to? In the future, our capacity to steward our votes and our capital, and to make sense of what's happening in the world, will all be titrated by superintelligences. And I worry that specs like the Claude Constitution are not shaping these ASIs to truly be my personal advocates and guardian angels.

And can we get them aligned to anything in the first place? Ryan and I had a long debate about whether the kind of reward hacking we saw with the OAI/Hugging Face hack extrapolates to superintelligences that would team up to literally take over the world.

The first piece of advice you get when you're learning to drive is that it will go much smoother if you look at the horizon instead of directly in front of your tires. And so it is with the trajectory of AI. Hope you enjoy!

Team, it is bittersweet to share that I’ll be moving on from OpenAI to start something new. It has been the honor of my life to help bring us to this point, and to do it alongside all of you.

I joined OpenAI in 2018, eight years ago this month, because I wanted to work on something hard. @sama introduced me to @gdb and @ilyasut, who showed me a pitch deck suggesting that because models improve predictably with scale, AGI was not only possible but likely. If you had told me then that we’d be where we are today, I wouldn't have believed you.

In the years that followed, I had the privilege of building the first versions of most of our operations and business teams – from Finance to Legal, People, CorpSec, GTM/Gov, Partnerships, and more. Among the most rewarding parts of this journey for me has been watching each of these teams mature under brilliant leaders. I am excited for the next decade in the hands of this incredibly capable team.

At the same time, we grew from a small research lab to one of the most consequential companies of our time. I was reminded of that fact constantly – from serving our first user to our billionth, to the growing scale and ambition of our partnerships and the occasional curveball (the Blip, etc.).

Through it all, I’m proud of how we’ve maintained our focus on people. It always amazes me how quickly the world has adopted our tools and rallied behind our mission. I hope we will continue to earn their trust.

content:
Deep dive into AI text-watermarking and what EU's AI Act actually mandates about AI detectability.

How it works: 
The SynthID paper from Demis and team in Nature is probably the best primer in the technology. Generally, most approaches involve sampling next tokens statistically differently with some random key while not distorting the semantics of the output.

Detecting text watermarks can never be perfect. Longer passages are always easier to detect, only at ~400 tokens do you get a true positive of rate of ~90% when your false positive rate is <1%. Because small changes in the text can change whether the algorithm thinks it's AI or not, other approaches include semantic data in their watermarking scheme too. 

Industry status on the EU regulation:
EU's AI Act Article 50(2) requires AI generations from all modalities to be AI-detectable, with practical implementation details still being finalized. The main exception is  "AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data" although how they would distinguish between these cases is unclear. Article 113 says "It shall apply from 2 August 2026."

Claude declared that they will comply. Gemini already uses SynthID for their text outputs (even though no production public detector exists for text outputs). OpenAI had developer watermarking a while ago but reportedly shelved it when 30% of their users said they'd use the product less. However, their support page says "our goal is to expand provenance signals to all modalities including text" (!)

I've always maintained I think it's critical to know whether text comes from AI or a human (and thus support tech like Pangram). Judging by the comments on X, I might be in the minority. This comment sort of embodies the backlash: "I'm paying it to write for me in a way people and machines wouldn't detect it is AI written" In other words, users believe if their ideas go into using AI for expressing them, *they* should be given credit for the idea and not penalized for using AI. I'd counterclaim that penalization and provenance are distinct, and provenance is extremely critical because
a) without provenance, you are more likely to be judged poorly and falsely accused of using AI when you didn't
b) just like with food, fundamentally readers deserve the right to know where the text came from and reserve their own judgment on whether its still valuable to them or not!

「AIで作ったんでしょ」というウザい問いに対する模範解答を解説していきますね。

まず、「そうです」とも「違います」とも答えてはいけません。

答えた時点で、相手の術中にハマるからです。

「違います」と答えた瞬間、

すると次に、

「本当に？」  
「証拠は？」

content:
「AIで作ったんでしょ」というウザい問いに対する模範解答を解説していきますね。

まず、「そうです」とも「違います」とも答えてはいけません。

答えた時点で、相手の術中にハマるからです。

「違います」と答えた瞬間、

――私はあなたに、自分の制作工程について説明する立場にあります。

という前提に同意することになるからです。

すると次に、

「本当に？」  
「証拠は？」  
「制作過程は？」

が始まります。

――では、証拠を出せば終わるのか？

終わりません。

AIを「使った」ことは、履歴などから証明できる場合があります。

しかし、  AIを「使っていない」ことを完全に証明するのは非常に難しい。

ラフを出しても、  
「後から作ったのでは？」

制作動画を出しても、  
「映っていないところでAIを使ったのでは？」

と、いくらでも疑い続けることができます。

これは、

――「ないことを証明せよ」という、いわゆる悪魔の証明です。

では、どうやって無実を証明すればいいのか？

と、ここで、その問いを考え始めた時点で負けています。

考えるべきなのは、

「どう証明するか？」

ではありません。

――なぜ、私が証明しなければならないのか？

です。

「AIを使った」と疑惑を提示したのであれば、まずその根拠を示すべきなのは疑った側でしょう。

疑われたというだけで、疑われた側に無実を証明する義務が発生するわけではありません。

ですが、これでもまだ、相手の術中にいます。

――そもそも、彼らは何の権限があって、他人の制作工程を審理しているのでしょうか？

突くべきは、ここ。

規約で生成AIが禁止されているコンテストの運営なら分かります。
AI不使用を条件に仕事を依頼した依頼主でも分かります。
そこには先に、規約や契約があるからです。

しかし、何の規約も契約もない第三者が、

「AIを使ったの？」  
「使っていないなら証明して」

と要求する。

これは相手の立証責任以前の問題です。

――誰があなたを裁判官として認めたのでしょうか？

権限のない問いに、わざわざ潔白を延々と説明する必要などありません。

「AIを使ったんでしょ」に丁寧に答えるなら、

「あなたに、私の制作工程の開示を要求する権利はありませんよ」

日常的に言うなら、もっと簡単に。

「なんであなたに説明しないといけないんですか？」

相手はこの問いに答えられません。

ですから、これが『模範解答』です。

content:
Claude Codeのトークン足りない問題。私はモデルを戻し忘れ、簡単な作業もFableに任せて無駄にしがち…実はこれ、Anthropicが解決策を出してた。「賢いモデルが仕切り、雑用は複数のHaikuに並列で投げる」形。プロンプト一発で設定できて、後はClaudeが勝手に振り分けてくれるのでオススメ。詳細は↓

【1. できるようになること】

一番賢いモデルを選んでいても、雑用を頼んだら、Claudeが判断して安いモデルに作業を振り分けてくれます。

ユーザー側がわざわざモデルを切り替えなくていいので、戻し忘れも起きません。

たとえば、こんなケースです。

Opusで作業している最中に「原稿2本を突き合わせて、特定の表現を全部拾い出す」という雑用が出てきた場合。これが勝手に安いモデルへ回って、30秒ほどで結果だけ返ってきます。使ったのは約25,000トークンくらい。

Opusのまま処理していたら、単価は5倍。
さらに言えば、読み込んだ原稿の中身がOpusの会話に残り続けて、そのあとのやりとり全部に乗ってしまいます。これが意外とトークン消費を増長させます。

【2. どういう仕組みか】

Anthropicが、Haiku 4.5の発表の時に提唱していた、以下の仕組みを再現しています。

「賢いモデルが複雑な問題を段階的な計画に分解し、複数のHaikuのチームを指揮して、サブタスクを並列で片づける」

モデルを選び直すのではなく、役割を分ける。
自分は指揮に専念して、手を動かす作業は安いモデルに渡します。部下は別の場所で作業して、結果だけ返してくる。

安いモデルに任せて大丈夫か？と思うかもですが、いまのHaikuはそこまで非力じゃないです。

・実務的なコーディング課題のベンチマークで73.3%
・速度は上位モデル比で最大4〜5倍
・価格は最上位の10分の1

で、効くところが2つあって、2つ目が本命です。

1つ目はシンプルです。品質差の出ない作業を、10分の1の単価で処理できるようになります。

2つ目は、部下（Haiku）が読んだ中身は指揮者（賢いモデル）の会話に残らないことです。ここが地味に大きい。
指揮者が自分で大量に読み込むと、その中身は以降のやりとりのたびに乗り続けます。
序盤にちょっと調べただけのつもりが、後半の往復すべてに上乗せされている。
長い作業ほど効いてきます。下請けに出すと、これが起きません。

【3. 使い方】

リプ欄のプロンプトを貼って、あとはClaudeと話しながら作ります。
貼ると、Claudeが環境を確認して、必要なファイルを作り、設定に足していきます。
既存の設定を壊さないよう、先にバックアップを取らせています。
途中で「これは既にありますが、どうしますか」と聞いてくることもあるので、そこだけ答えれば終わりです。

入るのは2つ。

①雑用を任せる部下と、②噛み合っていないときに教えてくれる番犬です。

部下には、「探す・読む・数える・整える」作業だけを渡します。判断と文章づくりは渡しません。
権限も読み取りだけにして、ファイルの書き換えはさせない。ここを緩くすると何でも安いモデルに流れて、品質が落ちます。

番犬の方は、送信のたびに裏で照合して、噛み合っていないときだけ「モデルを上げませんか」「これは部下に投げませんか」と言ってきます。

あとは今までどおり使うだけ。「これは安いモデルでやって」と指示する必要はありません。

【4. 注意点】

完全な自動化ではありません。振り分けを判断しているのはClaude自身なので、取りこぼすことがあります。その抜けを拾うのが番犬の役割です。
番犬自体は作業は止めず、コメントをしてくれるだけです。

content:
AIエージェントに、自分自身の「感情（に相当する内部信号）」に従って行動を選ばせると、仕事の成績が大幅に上がったという報告です。

LLMの内部では、"喜び"や"不安"、"混乱"といった感情に対応する27種類の計算パターンが生じていることが近年わかってきました。

研究者らは、エージェントが「次の手順」を選ぶ"直前"にこのパターンを読み取り、「いま自分は自信がある状態か、混乱状態か」を判断材料に加える仕組みを作りました。
さらに、作業の途中で内部状態が"急変"した瞬間を記録しておき、「どの手順のどこでつまずいたか」を特定して手順書を書き直すことにも活用。

すると、買い物サイトの操作や家事をさせる実験で、成功率が最大47ポイント以上も向上しました。
特に、「失敗からの立て直し」が頻繁に必要なタスクほど効果が大きかったそうです。
「混乱」を、失敗のサインが画面に現れるより先に検出できるとのこと。

なお、この「内部パターン」と選ばれる手順の組み合わせには"意味的なまとまり"が確認されており、単なる統計的な偶然ではなさそうとの見方がされています。

モデルの内部状態は、これまで安全性の研究などに使われてきましたが、こうした研究からエージェントの「意思決定」に役立つ資源にもなるかもしれません。

（AIが実際に感情を「感じている」という話ではなく、あくまで人間の感情表現を学習した結果として生じる、測定可能な内部の数値パターンです）

Think about a normal publishing workflow. The image gets exp
content:
An AI-generated image can be properly marked when it leaves the generator, and still lose that information before anyone actually sees it.

Think about a normal publishing workflow. The image gets exported from the AI tool, resized by a designer, uploaded to a CMS, downloaded again, and eventually reposted to social media.

Every one of those steps can change the file.

The EU AI Act introduces requirements for certain AI-generated content to carry machine-readable information that helps identify it as AI-generated or manipulated. But checking the original file only tells you that the process worked at the beginning.

The more useful question is whether that information survives all the way to the version your audience receives.

So test the actual workflow. Check the image after export, after editing, after upload, and after reposting. If the AI marking disappears somewhere along the way, record where it happened and keep another verification path back to the original asset.

Because the file your AI tool created is rarely the file people eventually see.

Transparency needs to survive the journey too.

''How Axis Robotics simulation can help solve one of the biggest problems of Physical AI robot training data''

Most interesting thing is that @axisrobotics  allows people to teleoperate robots directly within a browser-based simulation. This does not require a physical robot or special hardware.

Instead of collecting each demonstration with a real robot, Axis uses simulation as a scalable data-generation layer. Different tasks can be performed, the environment can be changed & a large number of robot trajectories can be generated.

This is important because building a general-purpose robot requires a lot of & diverse data. Data collection with a real robot is expensive, time-consuming & limited by the number of robots and operators.

Axis also focuses on data quality. The collected trajectories can be cleaned, validated, and augmented before being used in training. As a result, robot policy can learn from demonstrations of better quality.

Important thing here is Sim2Real. The data generated or collected in simulation is not just for simulation. AXIS is creating the entire pipeline 🔻

Simulation ➡️ Training ➡️ Real robot deployment

The biggest takeaway for us:

Axis is not just using simulation to test robots. They are turning simulation into a scalable training-data engine that can be used to build more general & capable robots. @AxisRoboticsBD

content:
The method for extracting encrypted reasoning from frontier models has been circulating for at least six months. A recent viral PDF, despite many errors and false claims, has made this technique outside the circle. It is a universal decryptor of any encrypted reasoning blocks.

It is surprising that both OpenAI and Anthropic chose an “encryption” that is cryptographically weak. It is a user-agnostic, model-agnostic stateless encryption and signature. If I were to design this, I would at least check the encrypted reasoning against a session ID and a model ID to prevent replay attacks. 

However, preventing CoT distillation may be fundamentally hard because models can read the encrypted thought anyway and a model smart enough can encode its replayed thoughts so that simple output checks cannot discover it.

This is partly why some investors have re-evaluated frontier model companies due to diffusion of technology. It is hard to distill from an NVIDIA chip, but model distillation is much easier. Even my introductory open source book “AI Agents in Depth” has an experiment of CoT distillation.

By the way, the server-side security of Codex and Claude Code are also very weak that people can simply extract APIs from subscriptions. There are a lot of model routers that provide 1/10 to 1/5 of API pricing by utilizing subscription pools.  These model routers often store agent traces and utilize the aforementioned CoT distillation techniques to extract training data.

This paper “Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs” is insane and contains a lot of details. Maybe the best security paper of 2026!

Deep Research Skill for Claude Code is a research engine that produces citation-backed reports with source credibility scoring, multi-provider search, and automated validation.

Dyna-2 is out and it's 🔥

Here's what that means in plain terms.

Dyna-2 was pre-trained on ONE MILLION hours of egocentric human video, 170 years of continuous human experience, cooking, folding, assembling, cleaning. 

And as that human data scaled, robot performance improved. Predictably. Monotonically. Across 39 tasks on two different robot embodiments the model had never seen.

→ 1,000 hours pre-training → 20% normalised task performance 
→ 10,000 hours → 28% 
→ 100,000 hours → 45% 
→ 1,000,000 hours → 53%

Human video exists at effectively unlimited scale. Every cook, every factory worker, every craftsperson wearing a camera is generating training data for future robots.

But the finding that stunned even the researchers, world modeling is what makes the transfer work. A model trained to predict future video AND actions massively outperforms one trained on actions alone. Video is the new scaling axis for robotics.

One more jaw-dropping data point. 13 minutes of teleoperation data was enough to fine-tune Dyna-2 to open a bottle cap using two five-fingered robot hands.

content:
重要なご指摘だと思います。 
おっしゃるとおり、外部事業者のサーバを利用する点では、生成AIも、メール、OneDrive、各種SaaSも地続きの問題です。 
私も確定的な答えを持っているわけではありません。 

私なりには、外部サービスへの秘密情報の入力が、刑法134条1項の「秘密を漏らした」に当たるのか、当たるとすれば「正当な理由」があるのか、という二段階で考える必要があると思っています。 

個人情報保護法上のクラウド例外は外部サーバへの送信だけで直ちに第三者への「提供」となるわけではないという点で参考になります。 
他方、生成AIは入力内容の解析自体がサービスの中核なので、単なる保管等と比べ外部事業者に秘密を漏らしていないと説明することは難しくなるように思います。 
従来のクラウドサービスとの違いはここにあると考えています。

仮に漏示に当たるなら、規約の確認、学習利用の拒否、匿名化、依頼者の同意、アカウント管理、事業者の信頼性などを踏まえ、「正当な理由」の有無を判断することになるのではないでしょうか。 
日弁連の「弁護士業務における生成AIの利活用等に関する注意事項」や「情報セキュリティを確保するための基本的な取扱方法について」も、守秘義務違反とならなくなる法的構成を明示していませんが、このように理解すると整合的に読めるように思います。 

とはいえ、「正当な理由」部分を主戦場にしてしまうと、あらゆるデータをAIに共有して判断を迅速化・高度化するというAIの美点が失われますので、個人的には漏示に当たらないようAIの構成を組むのが望ましいと考えています。

今回の透かしが新たな守秘義務問題を生むわけではありません。 
ただ、AI利用が事後的に検証され得るようになることで、従来から曖昧だった問題を士業として先送りしにくくなるというのが私の問題意識です。 
私はAIやクラウドを排除すべきだとは考えていません。 
むしろ、士業が安心して十分に活用できるよう法的・技術的な条件を明確にすることが重要だと思っています。

content:
ザハロワ氏の発言と
熊本日日新聞の記事

かつての枢軸国であった2カ国は7月、1945年に強制的に廃止させられた慣行を同時に復活させた。

ドイツ連邦議会は、連邦警察に関する新法を可決した。これは1994年以来、同警察にとって最大規模の改革となる。

連邦警察は、駅や空港でのリアルタイム顔認識、群衆の行動に関するAI分析、容疑の根拠なしでの身分証明書の確認、電話の盗聴、ドローンの運用といった新たな権限を付与された。

欧州最大のインターネット協会（ECO）は、この法律を「デジタルによる大規模監視の先駆け」と評した。電子フロンティア財団（EFF）は、この法律が、政府が生体認証による監視を行わないことを約束したドイツ自身の法律に真っ向から矛盾していると警告した。

戦後のドイツ連邦共和国の法制度は、警察と諜報機関を厳格に分離するという原則に基づいて構築されてきた。それはまさに、警察が諜報機関と化すと何が起こるかを、ドイツ人が自らの経験から痛感していたからである。今や、この分離は解体されてしまった。

『The Berliner』紙は次のように記している。「これらの改革は、ナチス政権下やシュタージによる監視に関する歴史的記憶に基づいて形成された憲法上の保障を損なっている」。ドイツのメディアでは以前、さらに厳しい表現も見られた。「ナチス政権以来、ドイツにこれほどの監視体制は存在しなかった。この背景に比べれば、ファイルや近所の密告者を抱えていた東ドイツのシュタージでさえ、素人じみている」。

かつての同盟国である日本でも同様のスキャンダルが発生している。熊本日日新聞は、東京近郊の朝霞基地に駐屯する陸上自衛隊の野戦情報部隊が、長年にわたり自国民を監視していた事実を暴いた。約50～60人で構成された特別チームは、日本国内の民間人に関する個人ファイルの作成に従事していた。そのファイル――いわゆる「個人BSD（basic source data）」――には、氏名、写真、個人情報、家族や財務に関する情報が含まれていた。「日本および自衛隊に対する態度」という項目も設けられていた。

以前、日本の裁判所はすでに、このような活動が違法であるとの判決を下していた。当時は、軍が文字通り市民の忠誠心を評価していたのだ。そして今、日本は次の段階へと進んだ――スパイ対策法である。入手可能な情報によると、この法律は、外国政府から資金提供を受けている人物の登録や、国民に対する広範な裁判外盗聴を規定しているという。

日本軍が最後に市民の忠誠度に関するファイルを作成したのは、昭和天皇の時代だった。当時、特高（特高警察）は、人々の政治的信条を理由に監視、逮捕、拷問を行っていた。

以前の体制が崩壊してから81年が経過した今、ベルリンと東京は足並みを揃えて動いている。敗戦した侵略国における戦後の国内秩序は、自国民に対する大規模な監視手段を排除するという原則に基づいて構築されていた。そのような監視は、強制収容所、ジェノサイド、そして人体を用いた残虐な実験が行われていた当時、ナチスにとって重要な手法の一つであった。

最後に、これと類似した暴力機構として知られていたのは、ゲシュタポと特高であった。これは私自身の比較ではなく、ドイツ人や日本人自身――彼らの専門家やマスコミ――が行っている比較である。東京とベルリンは、双方の指摘を無視している。さあ、動き出した。

MacBookなどの低リソース環境で「Muse Glimmer 30B」を動かすとき、高速化を狙って「DFlash drafter」を導入すると、かえって処理が遅くなってしまうことがあるそうです！💻

DFlash drafterは、RTX 3090やDGXのようなハイエンドなGPUでたくさんの余剰計算リソース（スペックの余裕）がないと、十分にスピードが上がらない仕組みになっているみたいですね。

・`--spec-draft-n-max` を「2〜3」あたりに小さくしてみる（8などの大きい値だとオーバーヘッドが増えてしまいます！）
・温度（temperature）や top-p、top-k のパラメータを細かく微調整する
・`--spec-type ngram-mod` への変更を検討する
・`-fit off` や `--no-warmup` を活用して無駄なオーバーヘッドを削る

ちなみに受容率はタスクによっても変わるもので、コード生成のような決まったパターンが多い処理だと効果が出やすいとのこと！

content:
Six and a half years ago, one OpenAI employee used 100,000 tokens a month and the whole company thought it was absurd. Today that number is the global average.

The interesting part isn't the token count. It's what changed underneath it — usage didn't grow because people got better at writing prompts. It grew because AI stopped being something you had to go ask, and started being something running in the background of everything you already do.

Same shift, smaller surface. Nobody's inbox used to run on AI either. You wrote the follow-up, built the tracker, opened the ticket, all by hand, one tool at a time.

Revo is built on the same bet Altman's math implies — that the ceiling isn't how smart the model is, it's how much of your actual work it's watching. Emails, meetings, Slack, tickets. Not a chat window you remember to open. A background process that already knows what needs doing before you ask.

The five-million-fold jump isn't really about tokens. It's what happens once AI stops waiting for you to show up.

content:
Sam Altman's 10-person billion-dollar company always gets summarized the same way: fewer humans, more agents, same output.

What gets left out is memory.

A 100-person company doesn't run on any one person's brain. It runs on shared context — who's talking to which client, what got promised on which call, what's already been tried. Cut the headcount to 10 and you don't just lose hands. You lose the people who used to hold all of that.

Revo replaces the holding, not just the doing.

It reads across email, meetings, Slack and tickets — not to summarize them, but to remember them. One shared brain the whole team pulls from. So when a teammate needs the tracker, or a client asks about a case someone else owns, the answer isn't "let me check." It's already there.

Then it goes one step further and turns what it remembers into action — drafted follow-ups, ready-to-send replies. You just review and tap "do it."

That's the hard part of the small-team-big-company math. Not doing more. Remembering everything, for everyone, all the time.
